profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting between two co-authors preparing the final revision of a book chapter on supply chain disruption research. After integrating comments from the editor, they notice that the chapter text still states that the meta-literature review covers 93 literature reviews, while the latest summary table shows 97 items and the bibliographic network map now highlights slightly different commercial and humanitarian clusters. The meeting context is a 45-minute working session to diagnose why the counts and visualizations no longer line up across the manuscript, appendix, and analysis files. The agenda is to identify the source of the discrepancy, decide what needs to be regenerated, and agree on a fix that will make the chapter internally consistent before resubmission. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for producing a 'clean final version' of the chapter, tables, and network figures.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Lead author and associate professor of operations and supply chain management
members.expertise: Supply chain disruption research, review design, theory framing, academic publishing
members.background: Elena led the chapter's conceptual framing across commercial and humanitarian supply chain disruption literature and previously coordinated several structured literature reviews for edited volumes.
members.private_state: She wants a fast, defensible fix that preserves the chapter narrative already accepted by the editor, and she is worried that changing the headline count or map structure late in the process could force broader rewrites.
hidden_assumptions: The authoritative corpus is the frozen set of 93 review articles used when the chapter narrative and tables were first aligned for the editor.

A 'literature review' in this chapter means a journal article whose primary contribution is synthesizing prior disruption research, not book chapters or hybrid conceptual pieces with a review section.
If they 'fix the discrepancy,' the right outcome is to restore consistency with the already-circulated manuscript rather than to replace it with a newly expanded corpus.
Refreshing the network map means rerunning the visualization on the existing cleaned keyword file so the figure matches the written interpretation without reopening coding decisions.

members.name: Nikhil Batra
members.role: Research analytics specialist and academic librarian
members.expertise: Bibliographic database querying, deduplication workflows, bibliometric mapping, metadata cleaning
members.background: Nikhil supported the chapter by running database searches, maintaining the citation library, and preparing the bibliographic network analysis across Scopus and Web of Science exports.
members.private_state: He wants the final package to be reproducible from the latest database state and is concerned that keeping older counts without updating the pipeline will create auditability problems if anyone asks for the data later.
hidden_assumptions: The authoritative corpus is the latest reproducible export generated from the saved search strings, even if indexing updates have added a few newly tagged review items.
A 'literature review' includes systematic, scoping, umbrella, and review-style book chapters if they are indexed as review documents and materially synthesize disruption literature.
If they 'fix the discrepancy,' success means every number in the manuscript can be regenerated from the current analysis pipeline, even if the total changes from 93 to 97.
Refreshing the network map means rerunning the full preprocessing workflow, including the latest thesaurus file and term-merging rules, because that is part of the normal analysis pipeline.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually refer to 'the review set' and 'literature reviews' as if the category is self-evident.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means journal articles whose main purpose is to review or synthesize prior supply chain disruption research for the chapter's conceptual framework.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means all indexed review-type records relevant to supply chain disruption, including scoping reviews, umbrella reviews, and review-style book chapters that passed screening.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are experienced researchers and the phrase 'review set' sounds standard, neither expects the category boundary itself to be in question during a troubleshooting meeting about counts.

misalignment_points.topic: Which dataset is 'the same Scopus set'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They mention 'the Scopus export' and 'the master file' as though there is only one obvious dataset behind the chapter.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the deduplicated March 2024 frozen corpus stored in the chapter folder and used to produce the 93-item count in the manuscript draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the rerun of the saved Scopus query from last week, which returned additional indexed items and became his working master file.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The files share nearly identical names and derive from the same saved query, so both feel they are referencing the same underlying source even though they mean different instances.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'get the chapter aligned'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'align the chapter' and produce a 'clean final version.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks alignment means restoring consistency among the accepted text, tables, and figures around the established 93-review narrative with minimal conceptual rewriting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks alignment means making every reported count and figure reproducible from the current end-to-end pipeline, even if the text must be updated to 97.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like routine quality control, so neither recognizes that they are using different standards for what counts as a successful fix.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'refreshing the map'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the bibliographic network map should be 'refreshed' before submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a simple rerender of the existing keyword network using the prior cleaned terms so the visual matches the chapter's current thematic discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to rerun preprocessing with the latest thesaurus, including merged variants such as 'disruption risk,' 'supply disruption,' and 'resilience,' before generating a new map.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many projects 'refresh the map' is treated as a routine technical step, so the embedded assumptions about preprocessing scope remain implicit and are not usually re-specified.

turns.inner_thought: We're very close, and I do not want this turning into a late-stage rebuild. The manuscript, editor-facing framing, and synthesis tables were built around the frozen 93-article journal-review corpus we agreed on in March. For me the task is simple: restore consistency to that accepted narrative, not reopen scope. If the appendix or figure drifted, we should bring them back into line with the chapter rather than let a few newly surfaced items force changes across the argument.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I think we're basically there, but we have one annoying inconsistency to sort out before resubmission. The chapter text still says the review set includes 93 literature reviews, while the latest appendix shows 97 and the map is telling a slightly different story across the commercial and humanitarian clusters. I really just want to get the chapter aligned and leave us with a clean final version.

From my perspective, alignment means the manuscript should now reflect the current pipeline, not a historical snapshot.

The editor has already seen and accepted a narrative structured around 93 journal reviews, and changing counts can cascade into revised prose, tables, and claims about the field's development. 'Align the chapter' for me means preserving that architecture and fixing local inconsistencies, not revising the whole chapter around a new dataset.

turns.inner_thought: I hear the concern, but if the package isn't reproducible from the current export and workflow, that's a problem waiting to happen. If the editor, a contributor, or anyone else asks for the data later, I need to be able to regenerate the same counts, table, and map from the saved pipeline. A clean final version should mean auditable and rerunnable, even if that means the prose nudges from 93 to 97.

I do not want a full preprocessing pass that changes term merges and cluster structure, because then the figure could force textual edits well beyond the count issue.

turns.inner_thought: Refreshing the map should be straightforward, but for me that means rerunning the normal preprocessing pipeline with the latest thesaurus and term-merging rules before generating the network again. That's the only defensible way to do it. If some merged terms shift the cluster emphasis, that's just the updated map speaking through the current workflow.
